The police and fire have been switching to a standard called P25. It offers some nice features, like better use of bandwidth (more people can talk on the same frequencies), and GPS location (for dispatch). It's digital, and the features make it possible for things like one officer calling another, or officers talking to dispatch without everyone else on the channel having to hear it.

With the internet being available and radio unencrypted, there have been some problems. It's easier for criminals to monitor online streams, and there are people who are trying to target victims of crimes.

With the early deployments of P25, there were significant issues with unencrypted communications. Some devices would lose keys upon losing power (no flash memory, or for security reasons). Sometimes there were bugs, etc. As such, many departments were configuring radios to accept any unencrypted transmission. Unencrypted transmissions were subject to spoofing and interception, so that's bad. Potentially really bad.

... and that brings us to why fire departments are being effectively forced to encrypt.

To avoid issues with unencrypted radios, newer systems and devices are often configured to reject any non-encrypted transmission. That includes (for example) fire departments with unencrypted channels.

Solution? Encrypt the fire channels, too, and the police and fire can now talk to each other.
